s: A recent graduate has just received her first credit card and a car loan offer. She has heard that credit cards 'build credit' but is nervous about debt. She says a friend paid $900 in interest on a $3,000 balance last year.
You are meeting with the client (judge). She wants to understand how credit cards and car loans differ, how to avoid unnecessary interest, and how late payments affect her.
p: Explain why credit card interest rates tend to be higher than rates for secured loans, such as automobile loans
Describe how a credit card user can minimize interest charges on credit card purchases
Investigate what happens to a low introductory interest rate when the borrower misses a payment or makes a late payment
n: Credit cards are unsecured, so lenders face more risk and charge higher rates
Pay the full statement balance each month and use the grace period
A missed or late payment can end the promotional rate and add fees
q: Which would you choose first, the credit card or the car loan, and why?
How does a credit score change the rate she is offered?

c: a credit union's member services team
s: A member has begun working part time and receives $1,100 per month. He has no savings and wants to buy a laptop for school in six months. He also worries about unexpected expenses.
You are meeting with the member (judge). He wants to learn how to set a savings goal, where to keep his savings, and how to build an emergency fund.
p: Explain the benefits of setting a specific savings goal
Describe how different savings accounts compare for short-term savings
Describe the purpose of an emergency fund and how much to aim for
n: A specific amount and date turns a wish into a plan
Compares savings accounts, interest, fees and access
An emergency fund covers unexpected expenses; aim for several months of costs over time
q: How much should he save each month for the laptop?
What would you do if he has to use his emergency savings?

s: A college freshman receives $1,500 per month from a part-time job and a scholarship. He has run out of money before the end of each of the last two months, mostly because of food delivery, subscriptions and impulse purchases.
You are meeting with the student (judge). He wants to understand how to create a budget, how to tell needs from wants, and how to track spending.
p: Explain how a budget helps a person manage spending
Distinguish between needs and wants in making spending decisions
Describe methods for tracking spending and adjusting a budget
n: A budget compares income to planned expenses and savings
Needs are required to live and learn; wants are optional
Apps, spreadsheets or envelopes help track; review and adjust monthly
q: Which subscription or expense would you cut first?
What if his income suddenly dropped?

c: a community library's personal finance workshop
s: A participant in her thirties has $5,000 saved and wants to start investing. She is worried about losing money and has heard about stocks, bonds and index funds but does not know the differences.
You are meeting with the participant (judge). She wants to understand risk and return, why diversification matters and how time affects investing.
p: Describe the relationship between investment risk and potential return
Explain how diversification reduces investment risk
Explain how time and compounding affect long-term investments
n: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
Spreading money across different investments lowers the impact of any one loss
Earning returns on returns grows money over time; starting early matters
q: Would you suggest she invest all $5,000 now? Why or why not?
What would you say if the market dropped 15% after she invested?

s: A young adult is buying a used car and has received three insurance quotes with very different premiums and deductibles. He is not sure what the coverage types mean and wonders if he can skip some coverage to save money.
You are meeting with the buyer (judge). He wants to understand how insurance works, how deductibles affect cost and which coverage is necessary.
p: Describe how a higher deductible affects insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs
Identify the types of auto insurance coverage and why each matters
n: Insurance pools risk so a person pays a premium instead of facing a large unexpected loss
A higher deductible usually lowers the premium but raises the cost of a claim
Liability, collision and comprehensive cover different risks; liability is usually required
q: Would you recommend a $500 or $1,500 deductible for him? Why?
What can he do to lower his premium without reducing coverage?
